en: I meditate daily upon that which shines as the meaning of the syllable *Oṃ*, radiant at the peak of the fourth *Oṃ*— the fourth of the fourth, the three-footed Rāma, who is pure self alone.

Oṃ. May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones. With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise you and attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods. May Indra, of far-reaching fame, grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel is unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!

Om. Then Paippalāda, Aṅgiras, and Sanatkumāra said to Atharvan: "O Blessed One, what meditation is to be employed at the beginning, and what is that which is to be meditated upon? What is that meditation, who is the meditator, and what is the object of meditation? To them, Atharvan replied: "The syllable 'Om'—this syllable is the meditation to be employed at the beginning and is that which is to be meditated upon. This syllable is the Supreme Brahman; its four feet are the four Vedas. Thus, this syllable is the four-footed Supreme Brahman."
The first syllable is the Earth, the letter *a*, [associated with] the Ṛg-verses, the Ṛgveda, Brahmā, the Vasus, the Gāyatrī meter, and the Gārhapatya fire.
The second is the Intermediate Space, that is the letter *u*, [associated with] the Yajus-formulas, the Yajurveda, Viṣṇu, the Rudras, the Triṣṭubh meter, and the Dakṣiṇāgni fire.
The third is Heaven, that is the letter *m*, [associated with] the Sāman-chants, the Sāmaveda, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Jagatī meter, and the Āhavanīya fire.

At the very end of this, the fourth half-mora is the syllable *oṃ*, which is the world of Soma; it is the Atharvaveda with its Atharvaṇa mantras, the Saṃvartaka fire, the Maruts, the Virāj, and the single seer. It is remembered as radiant, the first being reddish-yellow, having Mahābrahman as its deity;
the second is lightning-like and black, having Viṣṇu as its deity.
The third [syllable] is both auspicious and inauspicious, white, and has Rudra as its deity.
At the end of this [third syllable], there is a fourth half-mora; it is radiant, possesses all colors, and has Puruṣa as its deity.
This very Oṃkāra thus consists of four syllables, has four feet, four heads, and four morae; it is gross, being short, long, protracted, and [the fourth mora].

Having uttered "Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ" three times, the fourth [syllable] is the peaceful Self. Through the application of the *praṇava* as a flood, when the entire "Oṃ" is employed, the light of the Self revolves once; it revolves just by being uttered once. This very syllable is called *oṅkāra* because it carries one upward to the food (the state of nourishment). It is called *pralaya* because all vital breaths (*prāṇas*) dissolve therein. It is called *praṇava* because it leads all the vital breaths into the Supreme Self.
Established in the fourth state, it is the source of all gods and all wombs of existence; every expressible object has the *praṇava* as its essence. || 1 ||

He is called *deva* because he unites [all beings]; he is the *tāra* (savior) because he delivers one from all sufferings and fears; he is *viṣṇu* because all the gods enter into him; he is *brahmā* because he expands (*bṛhayati*) everything; he is *prakāśa* (light) because, like a lamp, he illuminates all internal objects of meditation; he is *vidyut* (lightning) because he flashes repeatedly within the body like lightning amidst the luminaries; and he is *vyāpī* (the Pervasive One), Mahādeva, because by piercing every direction, he pervades and causes all worlds to be pervaded. || 2 ||

The first *mātrā* is waking; the second is dreaming; the third is deep sleep; and the fourth is the *turīya*. Because one conquers all the quarters (*pāda*) completely through the *mātrās* that have reached their corresponding counterparts, it is self-luminous and becomes Brahman itself; thus, this is the means for attaining perfection and is employed at the beginning of meditation and other practices. Because it involves the withdrawal of all the instruments of perception and because it sustains [all], the *turīya* is Brahman.

Having established all the organs in the mind, Viṣṇu is the meditator; having established the vital breath along with the organs in the mind, Rudra is the meditator; having established the vital breath along with the organs at the end of the sound (nāda) within the Supreme Self, one meditates upon Īśāna, who is to be meditated upon. All this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the senses together with the elements—is produced from Him. He is not a cause, for He is the meditator of causes; indeed, as the meditator, He is the object of meditation.

Śambhu, endowed with all sovereignty, having fixed himself firmly in the midst of space for even a single moment longer [than that], obtains the entire fruit of seven thousand four hundred sacrifices, as well as the goal of Oṃ. Oṃ is the fruit of all meditation, yoga, and knowledge; Oṃ is the supreme Veda, the Lord, or Śiva alone, who is to be meditated upon as the bringer of auspiciousness. Abandoning everything else, a twice-born who has studied this entire Atharvaśikha is liberated from dwelling in a womb;
he is liberated from dwelling in a womb. This is the truth. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 3.
Oṃ, "May we hear with our ears what is auspicious"—this is peace.
Thus ends the Atharvaśikhopaniṣad belonging to the Atharvaveda.
